A spectroscopic indicator of blockage onset can only be a hypothesis, so the shortlist is conditional.

recommendations.rationale: ATR is a common in-line route for liquids and pastes and samples only a thin layer at the crystal, so a flush ATR probe would sense the layer next to the pipe wall, where deposits start. Mid-IR gives well-defined, selective absorption bands.
recommendations.conditions: The slurry must wet the ATR crystal and must not abrade or foul it.

citations.quote: suitability of analyzed samples for ATR measurements, which is true for liquid or soft solid samples and their components, allowing a tight contact with the probe head.
Vibrational spectroscopy in the mid-IR range (4000-400 cm-1) is one of the most informative methods of chemical analysis.

recommendations.rationale: Raman gives a molecular fingerprint and tolerates water better than infrared methods, so it is a natural single-method comparison for a likely aqueous slurry. Its signal is weak and can be swamped by fluorescence.
recommendations.conditions: Check the fluorescence background on real slurry samples.

citations.quote: Raman is particularly well-suited for aqueous environments, as it exhibits low absorbance for water molecules compared to infrared methods.

recommendations.rationale: NIR reflection is the most common in-line fiber-probe method and suits opaque, strongly scattering samples, so it would fit an optically thick slurry. Whether this slurry is scattering or transparent is unknown.
recommendations.conditions: Applies only if the slurry is optically thick and scattering rather than transparent.

citations.quote: Near-IR vibrational spectroscopy (NIR) is the most common online analysis method performed using fiber optic probes.
NIR Reflection is primarily used for opaque or highly concentrated dairy products, such as yogurt, butter, or whole milk concentrates.

measurement_concept.probe_and_geometry: A single in-line fiber probe at the pipe wall: a flush ATR head for MIR, or a Raman probe for the comparison. Geometry (contact ATR versus a windowed reflection or Raman probe) depends on the answers to Q1 and Q2.
measurement_concept.location: One measurement point on the transfer pipe, chosen where deposits or solids build-up would show first; access for cleaning must be confirmed (Q4, Q5).
measurement_concept.fiber_link: Mid-IR needs chalcogenide or polycrystalline fibers or hollow waveguides; Raman and NIR use silica fibers. No fiber length, product code or rating is stated in the sources and none is assumed here.

risks.risk: Line pressure and flow rate cannot be obtained from optical spectra, so the shortlist addresses only a possible blockage proxy, not the customer's first two targets.
If the slurry is optically thick or highly scattering, a contact ATR or Raman probe may see only a thin or local volume that does not represent the bulk stream.

chemometrics_note: Both candidate methods need chemometric models: MIR and Raman calibrations are specific to the sample matrix, and a blockage indicator would most likely be a classification model built on labelled samples. Reference data for the blockage state must come from the process, not from the spectra.
realtime_tracking_note: The early-warning goal is an in-line, time-resolved measurement: spectra would be acquired continuously at the probe and tracked against the model. The acquisition rate and the required warning lead time would have to be matched to the process.
future_direction: A later step could combine mid-IR ATR and Raman in one multispectral probe, since their spectra are complementary; any gain would still have to be shown against the best single method on independent runs.

proposal.what_would_change_it: If the lab trial shows the slurry is transparent, or that Raman detects a blockage-related change better than mid-IR ATR, the single-method choice would change. If pressure and flow are the real priority, no optical method applies and conventional sensors are needed.
proposal.next_step: Run a feasibility trial on representative slurry samples with the single methods, starting with a mid-IR ATR probe.

brief_answer: Line pressure and flow rate are not spectroscopic quantities, so fiber-optic spectroscopy cannot measure them; conventional pressure and flow sensors are needed. For blockage, an optical probe could be tested as a proxy: mid-IR ATR first, Raman as a comparison, and NIR reflection only if the slurry is optically thick. Whether any method sees blockage early enough is unknown and needs a lab trial on your slurry.
